title: When the Cipher Falls Revisited
premise: Retired detective Odile Iversen, who quietly solved three deaths the police ruled accidents, is paid a suspiciously large retainer by a nervous stranger to prove that a murder has not yet happened — the predicted killing of Judge Marren Hale, whose infamous 'Cipher Case' conviction Odile helped close twenty years ago. As Odile investigates, they discover the stranger is connected to the man Odile's testimony helped imprison, and that the original case was built on a memory Odile has never fully trusted. When the judge is found alive but a witness from the old trial turns up dead, Odile must decide whether loyalty to their former partner — who buried evidence — matters more than the truth. In the end, Odile exposes the real killer of the Cipher Case, prevents the judge's murder, and burns their own celebrated reputation to do it, choosing truth over the legend they built.
about_author: O. M. Crane is the pen name of a former court archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing misfiled evidence before turning to fiction. They live above a secondhand bookshop and claim every novel begins with a file that should have been destroyed.

chapters.title: The Retainer
chapters.summary: Odile Iversen, running a failing bookshop after retirement, receives an envelope of cash from a pale, trembling client named Wren Ashby, who asks them to prove a murder will not happen. The target: Judge Marren Hale. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: wary curiosity masking the itch of an unsolved thing.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present: Odile reviews the three 'accidental' deaths they privately solved, establishing their method and their silence. Their former partner, Detective Sorrel Vane, calls warning them off the new job. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: pride shadowed by guilt over what silence costs.

chapters.title: A Judge With Enemies
chapters.summary: Odile surveils Judge Hale, mapping his routines and finding a threatening note already in his chambers — dated before Wren ever walked into the shop. Someone else knows. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: dread tightening into purpose.

chapters.title: Wren's Alibi
chapters.summary: Odile confronts Wren about the pre-dated note; Wren admits to being the daughter of Elias Marsh, the man convicted in the Cipher Case Odile helped close. She wants the judge cleared of plotting revenge so her father can die believing justice held. POV: alternating Odile/Wren. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into doubt.

chapters.title: The Cipher Case, Reopened
chapters.summary: Odile rereads the old trial files and finds a gap in their own memory of the pivotal night — a witness statement they signed but cannot recall reading. POV: Odile, deep in recollection. Emotional beat: the ground shifting under one's own past.

chapters.title: Sorrel's Warning
chapters.summary: Former partner Sorrel Vane visits the shop, ostensibly friendly, actually probing how much Odile remembers. A loaded reference to 'the night at the boathouse' lands like a blade. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: loyalty and suspicion sharing one chair.

chapters.title: Dead Water
chapters.summary: Marguerite Doyle, the key witness from the original trial, is found drowned — ruled accidental. Odile recognizes the staging instantly. The prediction is coming true around its edges. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: cold fury.

chapters.title: The Bookshop Trap
chapters.summary: Someone searches the shop overnight; Odile, waiting, catches a hired hand who implicates a lawyer named Corben Tate — Hale's old prosecutor rival. First false lead. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: momentum, then the sting of a wrong turn.

chapters.title: Tate's Confession That Isn't
chapters.summary: Odile corners Tate, who produces his own alibi and drops a bombshell: he was paid years ago to lose a piece of evidence — by someone inside the police. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: vertigo as the conspiracy points inward.

chapters.title: What Odile Signed
chapters.summary: Odile tracks down the original boathouse statement and finds their own signature on a page describing events they now realize could not have witnessed. Memory or forgery? POV: Odile, fractured flashbacks. Emotional beat: self-distrust at its deepest.

chapters.title: Elias Marsh, Dying
chapters.summary: Odile visits the imprisoned Elias Marsh, who refuses exoneration talk but lets slip a detail only the true killer would know. He isn't protecting himself — he's protecting someone. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: pity tangled with alarm.

chapters.title: Wren Disappears
chapters.summary: Wren vanishes, leaving behind the retainer money untouched and a note: 'Ask Sorrel about the second set of keys.' The clock on the predicted murder accelerates. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: panic sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Second Set of Keys
chapters.summary: Odile discovers Sorrel had access to the boathouse the night of the original crime — and to Marguerite Doyle's building the week she died. Confrontation looms. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: grief for a friendship already dying.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Odile and Sorrel meet where it began. Sorrel admits burying evidence — not of Marsh's innocence, but of who really killed the Cipher victim: Hale's late wife, ruled a suicide. Sorrel claims he protected Odile's career. POV: dual. Emotional beat: heartbreak weaponized.

chapters.title: The Wife's File
chapters.summary: Odile pulls the sealed file on Hale's wife and finds the same staged-accident signature as the recent drowning. The killer has been active for twenty years, hiding inside the justice system itself. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: the pattern snapping into focus.

chapters.title: Hale's Secret
chapters.summary: Judge Hale confesses to Odile that he received anonymous letters proving his wife was murdered — and that he planned to name the killer publicly, which is why a death was predicted for him. He knows the name. POV: Odile/Hale. Emotional beat: two broken keepers of the same secret.

chapters.title: The Name in the Margin
chapters.summary: The letters' author is revealed: Marguerite Doyle herself, who witnessed the wife's murder and spent decades blackmailing the killer — until she tried to stop. The killer is the retired forensic examiner, Dr. Ilse Brandt, whose findings closed both cases. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: horror at how neatly evil wore procedure.

chapters.title: Finding Wren
chapters.summary: Odile deduces Brandt has taken Wren — the last person who can link the letters to the file — and traces them to the decommissioned records annex where the original evidence is stored. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into ferocity.

chapters.title: The Records Annex
chapters.summary: Climax: Odile confronts Brandt amid twenty years of misfiled proof. Brandt argues she merely corrected a corrupt system; Odile counters with the one thing Brandt cannot burn — the memory Odile finally recovered, complete. Wren is saved; Sorrel arrives to make the arrest real. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: truth as a physical act.

chapters.title: Exhumation
chapters.summary: Fallout: Brandt confesses under weight of evidence; Elias Marsh is exonerated posthumously eligible; Hale resigns rather than preside over the case. Sorrel faces charges for the buried evidence and doesn't blame Odile. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: justice arriving too late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: Wren returns the unspent retainer, asking instead for the truth in writing. Odile gives her the full account, including their own compromised memory — refusing the comfortable version. POV: Odile/Wren. Emotional beat: honesty as the only inheritance worth leaving.

chapters.title: The Shop at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Odile reopens the bookshop with a new sign: cold cases taken on request. A first customer walks in with a photograph and a question. The cipher falls; another one opens. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope.
